look_here_first: Start with the red-oak leaf architecture: large deciduous leaves with 5–9 deep bristle-tipped lobes and conspicuous tufts of hair in the vein axils beneath. Then confirm with the shallow saucer-shaped acorn cup covering only about one-quarter to one-third of the nut.

project_inclusion.range_basis: Williamson — University of Texas Williamson County flora documents Quercus shumardii. Travis — APHIS environmental documentation for a Travis County treatment area identifies Shumard oak among hardwoods in and surrounding the project woodlands. Bexar — a Bexar County environmental report for the Cibolo/Schertz project area identifies Shumard oak among prevalent native riparian/mesic woodland trees.
project_inclusion.range_guardrail: Exact county evidence only; historical Quercus shumardii var. texana records are not counted as Q. shumardii because that name has been applied to Texas red oak concepts.

best_field_traits: lower surface mostly glabrous except for conspicuous hair tufts in vein axils
terminal buds gray-brown and often noticeably 5-angled
acorns mature in the second year
acorn cup shallow saucer-shaped, covering about one-quarter to one-third of nut
FNA mature leaf blade usually 100–200 mm long; substantial overlap with other red oaks
ripe saucer/cup often 7–12 mm deep and 15–30 mm wide, generally enclosing 1/4–1/3 nut
morphology_keys.oak_training: Separate Shumard oak from Texas red oak by using the whole character set rather than leaf shape alone: Shumard generally has larger leaves, more mesic habitat, prominent vein-axil hair tufts beneath, and a broad shallow cup.

comparisons.key_distinctions: Quercus buckleyi is the common limestone upland red oak of Central Texas and often has smaller leaves and a drier-habitat profile. Q. muehlenbergii is a white-oak-group species with chestnut-like regularly toothed leaves lacking bristle tips. Q. polymorpha has mostly unlobed to shallowly toothed evergreen/semi-evergreen foliage and is not native to the project target zone.

best_tie_breakers: Mature Shumard cup often a broad saucer, enclosing only 1/4–1/3 nut; Buckley usually cup/goblet-like and proportionally deeper.
Shumard terminal buds 4–8 mm, often five-angled in cross-section and glabrous; Buckley bud scale margins often distinctly ciliate.
Shumard mature leaves often 100–200 mm long and mostly glabrous beneath except prominent lower vein-axil hair tufts; Buckley smaller on average, but can have small tufts as well.
unreliable_alone: Underside hair tufts (not exclusive to Shumard).
Single shade leaf or lobing count.
Tree height without acorn or bud confirmation.
diagnostic_comparison.hybrid_guardrail: Natural intermediates with Texas red oak are recognized; do not force an ID.
